title: Love, Beauty and Immortality: Symposium and Phaedo
subtitle: A drinking party about desire and a prison cell facing death: Plato's two most moving dialogues
era: c. 385–370 BCE (dialogues set in 416 and 399 BCE)
objectives: By the end you will be able to retell Aristophanes' myth of the split humans and explain what it says about love.
By the end you will be able to explain Diotima's account of love as desire for the good forever, and describe the ladder of love step by step.
By the end you will be able to explain what 'Platonic love' originally meant and how it differs from the modern phrase.
By the end you will be able to outline the main arguments for the immortality of the soul in the Phaedo and the objections raised by Simmias and Cebes.
By the end you will be able to connect both dialogues to Plato's theory of Forms.
hook:
Two scenes, set seventeen years apart. In the first, it is 416 BCE and the young poet Agathon has just won the prize for tragedy at the great Athenian festival. The morning after the celebrations, a group of friends gathers at his house, all slightly hungover. They agree to go easy on the wine and instead take turns giving speeches in praise of Love. Late in the night, a drunk and beautiful politician crashes through the door wearing a garland of ivy and violets.

In the second scene, it is 399 BCE. Socrates sits in an Athenian prison on the last day of his life (Day 10). His friends are weeping. He is calmly arguing that the soul cannot die, and that a philosopher should be glad to meet death. At sunset he drinks the hemlock.

The first scene is Plato's *Symposium*; the second is his *Phaedo*. One is about desire, the other about death. Yet they ask the same question: what in us reaches beyond this changing, mortal world, and where is it trying to go?

sections.heading: A Party Where Everyone Gives a Speech
sections.body:
A **symposium** (literally ‘drinking together’) was a real Greek institution: an evening party for men, held after dinner, with wine mixed with water, music, games and conversation. Plato turns one into a philosophical contest. The guests are real historical figures, among them the doctor Eryximachus, the young Phaedrus, Agathon himself, the comic playwright **Aristophanes**, and Socrates.

The story reaches us at several removes. A man named Apollodorus tells it years later, having heard it from Aristodemus, a devoted follower of Socrates who was there. This layering is typical of Plato. It reminds us that we are hearing a carefully constructed work of art, not a transcript.

It helps to know the social background. **Eros**, the Greek word for passionate love and desire (and the name of the god of love), was often discussed in the context of relationships between an older man and a younger one. Such relationships were an accepted, if regulated, part of upper-class Athenian life, and the early speeches take them for granted. Plato's dialogue begins inside this world and ends somewhere very different.

The first speakers praise Love in ways that reveal their own personalities. Phaedrus says Love makes people brave, since nobody wants to look like a coward in front of the one they love. Pausanias distinguishes a ‘heavenly’ love of the soul from a ‘common’ love of the body. Eryximachus, the doctor, turns Love into a cosmic force of harmony found in medicine, music and the seasons. Agathon delivers a gorgeous, flowery speech claiming Love is the youngest, most beautiful and most delicate of the gods. Each speech has something true in it, and each is incomplete.

sections.heading: Aristophanes: The Search for Our Other Half
sections.body:
The most memorable speech before Socrates belongs to Aristophanes, the comic genius who had mocked Socrates on stage years earlier in the *Clouds* (Day 9). Plato gives him a story that still shapes how people talk about love today.

Once upon a time, Aristophanes says, human beings were not as we are now. Each was round, with four arms, four legs and two faces looking in opposite directions. They moved by cartwheeling at great speed. There were three kinds: male-male, female-female and male-female. These original humans were so strong and proud that they tried to attack the gods. Zeus, not wanting to destroy them (who would then offer sacrifices?), decided to weaken them by cutting each one in half, like slicing an egg with a hair. Apollo turned their faces around and stitched up the wound, tying the skin at the navel, which we still carry as a reminder.

Ever since, each of us has been only half a person, searching for our missing other half. When two halves find each other, they are overwhelmed with love and never want to be apart. They cannot even say what they want from each other; they just want to be whole again. Love, Aristophanes concludes, is the name for the desire and pursuit of wholeness.

The myth is comic and absurd, yet strangely moving. It explains why love feels like recognition rather than choice, why people say they have found their ‘other half’, and why separation hurts like an injury. It also gives a story for different kinds of attraction, since some original humans were made of two males or two females. Notice what is missing, though. In Aristophanes' account, we love a particular person simply because they are *ours*, whether or not they are good. Socrates will challenge exactly this.

sections.heading: Diotima: Love Is a Hunger, Not a God
sections.body:
When Socrates' turn comes, he does something unusual. Instead of giving his own speech, he reports what he was taught as a young man by **Diotima**, a wise woman and priestess from Mantinea. Scholars disagree about whether Diotima was a real person; she appears nowhere else in ancient sources, and many think Plato invented her. Either way, it is striking that the deepest teaching on love in the dialogue is put in the mouth of a woman, in a room full of men.

First, Socrates questions Agathon in his usual style (the elenchus from Day 9). If Love is the desire for beautiful things, then Love must *lack* beauty, since nobody desires what they already have. So Love cannot be a beautiful god after all.

Diotima explains that Love is something in between: neither mortal nor god, but a **daimon**, a go-between spirit. She tells a myth of his birth. At a feast celebrating the birth of Aphrodite, Poros (Resource) got drunk on nectar, and Penia (Poverty) lay with him and conceived Love. So Love takes after both parents: always needy, barefoot and homeless like his mother, but also scheming, bold and resourceful like his father. Love is therefore like a philosopher, who is neither wise nor ignorant but loves and seeks wisdom. The word philosophy, after all, means ‘love of wisdom’.

What, then, does love really want? Diotima's answer: to possess the good forever. And since mortals cannot live forever, love seeks a substitute: to **give birth in beauty**, in body or in soul. Some people reproduce physically, leaving children behind. Others are ‘pregnant in soul’ and give birth to poems, laws and ideas. Think of the poems of Homer or the laws of Solon, Diotima says. Who would not rather have children like these, who win their parents undying fame? Love, on this view, is our mortal nature's reach for immortality.

sections.heading: The Ladder of Love
sections.body:
Diotima then reveals what she calls the final and highest mysteries, using language borrowed from religious initiation. Love properly guided rises step by step, like climbing a ladder. This passage is often called the **ladder of love**.

1. A young person first loves **one beautiful body**, and through that love produces beautiful words.
2. Then they realize that the beauty of one body is akin to the beauty of another, and so come to love **all beautiful bodies**, holding the passion for any single one more lightly.
3. Next they see that **beauty of soul** is more valuable than beauty of body, and can love a good person even if they are not physically attractive.
4. From souls they move to the beauty of **practices and laws**, the ways communities live well together.
5. Then to the beauty of **knowledge** of every kind, gazing at the vast ‘open sea’ of beauty.
6. Finally, suddenly, the lover catches sight of **Beauty itself**: beauty that is eternal, neither coming into being nor passing away, not beautiful in one respect and ugly in another, not a face or a body or a speech, but ‘itself by itself’, in which all beautiful things share.

You may recognize this last description. It is a **Form**, exactly as we met it on Day 11. The ladder of love is the Cave (Day 12) told in the language of desire: an ascent from particular, changing things to the unchanging reality they reflect. Only someone who has seen Beauty itself, Diotima says, can give birth to true virtue rather than images of it.

This is the origin of the phrase **Platonic love**. It was coined in the fifteenth century by the Italian scholar Marsilio Ficino, translator of Plato, to describe love that rises through a person toward the divine. Today the phrase usually means a friendship without sex, which is a thin echo of the original. For Plato, Platonic love is full of passion; it simply does not stop at the body.

Then the door bursts open. **Alcibiades**, brilliant and notorious, arrives drunk and gives a speech praising not Love but Socrates. He describes how he once tried to seduce Socrates and failed, and how Socrates endured winter cold barefoot on campaign at Potidaea. Socrates, he says, is like a cheap statue of a satyr that opens to reveal golden images of gods inside. The comic scene makes a serious point: Socrates is the living example of the lover who has climbed the ladder. Many readers also find something sad in it. Alcibiades loved Socrates the man, but never followed him upward. Some critics, most famously Martha Nussbaum, ask whether the ladder leaves behind something precious: the love of one irreplaceable person.

sections.heading: The Phaedo: Philosophy as Practice for Dying
sections.body:
Now jump to the prison. The *Phaedo* is narrated by Phaedo, one of the friends present on Socrates' last day. Plato tells us he himself was absent, ill. So this too is a constructed account, though the calm death it describes became one of the most influential scenes in Western history.

Socrates surprises his friends by saying that a true philosopher should welcome death. Why? Because philosophy, he says, is **practice for dying and being dead** (64a). Death is the separation of the soul from the body. And the philosopher's whole life has been an effort to free the soul from the distractions of the body: its hungers, fears, illnesses and the confusing reports of the senses. Pure knowledge of the Forms is reached by thought alone. So if the soul survives death, the philosopher is finally getting what he has spent his life seeking.

That ‘if’ is the problem, and his friends Simmias and Cebes, two visitors from Thebes, press it. Most people fear, Cebes says, that when the soul leaves the body it scatters like breath or smoke and is nowhere. Socrates offers several arguments in reply:

- **The cyclical argument.** Opposites come from opposites: the larger from the smaller, waking from sleeping. So the living come from the dead as the dead come from the living, and souls must exist somewhere in between.
- **The argument from recollection.** As in the *Meno* (Day 11), learning is really remembering. We recognize that two sticks are only imperfectly equal because we already know Equality itself, which we never saw in this life. So the soul existed before birth.
- **The affinity argument.** There are two kinds of things: visible, changing, composite things, and invisible, unchanging Forms. The body resembles the first kind; the soul, which grasps the Forms, resembles the second. So the soul is likely indestructible like them.
- **The final argument.** Some things always bring a property with them: fire always brings heat, so fire cannot admit cold. The soul always brings life to the body. So the soul cannot admit death; when death approaches, it withdraws, intact.

sections.heading: Objections, a Myth and a Rooster
sections.body:
The *Phaedo* is honest about how hard these arguments are. In the middle of the dialogue, Simmias and Cebes raise objections so strong that the listeners fall into despair.

Simmias offers the **harmony objection**. The attunement (harmony) of a lyre is invisible and beautiful, yet when the lyre is smashed, the harmony is destroyed too, even before the wood rots. Perhaps the soul is like that: the attunement of the body's elements, which vanishes when the body breaks. Socrates replies, among other things, that a harmony cannot oppose the instrument it depends on, yet the soul often resists and rules the body's desires.

Cebes offers the **weaver objection**. A weaver may wear out many cloaks in his lifetime, but he eventually dies, and the last cloak survives him. Even if the soul outlasts several bodies, how do we know it does not finally wear out? This is what pushes Socrates to give the final argument from the Forms.

At this crisis point, Socrates warns against **misology**, hatred of arguments. Just as someone betrayed by many friends may come to hate all people, someone let down by weak arguments may decide reasoning is worthless. The fault, he says, lies in our lack of skill, not in reason itself.

Socrates ends with a vivid myth about the afterlife and the true shape of the earth, saying no sensible person would insist it is exactly true, but that it is a fine risk to believe something like it. Then he bathes, says goodbye to his family, and drinks the poison. His last words, as Plato reports them, are a request that his friend Crito sacrifice a rooster (a cock) to Asclepius, a debt he must not forget. Asclepius was the god of healing. Some readers think Socrates meant that death was a cure for the illness of life; others, including Nietzsche, found that reading pessimistic; others think it was simply a pious debt. Phaedo closes by calling him the best, wisest and most just man of his time.

Are the arguments any good? Most philosophers today think none is decisive. Aristotle, as we will see on Days 16 and 19, would treat the soul as the form of a living body, much closer to Simmias' harmony than to Socrates' detachable soul.

keyQuote.text: Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; make this offering to him and do not forget.
keyQuote.source: Plato, Phaedo 118a, Socrates' last words (trans. G. M. A. Grube)

modernConnection.title: Soulmates, Dating Apps and Loving Someone Into Growth
modernConnection.body:
Aristophanes' myth is alive in every song about finding ‘the one’ and every dating profile searching for a ‘perfect match’. The idea that somewhere out there is a person who completes you is one of the most powerful romantic beliefs in modern culture, and dating apps quietly sell it: answer enough questions, and the algorithm will locate your other half.

Psychologists have studied this belief. The social psychologist C. Raymond Knee, in research beginning in the late 1990s, distinguished **destiny beliefs** (a relationship either is meant to be or it is not) from **growth beliefs** (relationships are built and developed through effort and challenges). People with strong destiny beliefs tend to be more likely to give up when problems appear, taking conflict as a sign they chose wrongly. People with growth beliefs are more likely to work through difficulties. In other words, Aristophanes' romantic picture may make love more fragile.

Diotima's view looks more like a growth theory. For her, love is not finding a missing piece but being drawn upward: loving someone makes you want to become better, create something good together, and see more of what is valuable in the world. Many people describe their best relationships exactly this way, as making them more generous and curious, not just complete.

The comparison also shows the limits of Diotima's ladder. Modern readers often worry that it treats the beloved as a stepping stone, valuable only as a route to something higher. Most of us want to be loved for who we particularly are, not as an example of Beauty. Perhaps a mature view of love needs both speeches: Aristophanes' insistence on this one irreplaceable person, and Diotima's insistence that love should make us grow. It is worth remembering that Plato put both views in the same room, and let neither speaker have the last word without a challenge.

vocabulary.definition: A Greek drinking party after dinner with wine, music and conversation; also the title of Plato's dialogue about love.
vocabulary.example: At Agathon's symposium, the guests agreed to drink moderately and give speeches about Love.

vocabulary.definition: The Greek word for passionate love or desire, and the name of the god of love; for Diotima, a needy spirit always reaching for what it lacks.
vocabulary.example: Diotima argues that eros cannot itself be beautiful, because we only desire what we do not have.

vocabulary.definition: In Greek religion, a spirit between gods and humans that carries messages between them; Diotima calls Love a daimon.
vocabulary.example: As a daimon, Love is neither mortal nor divine but always in between, like the philosopher between wisdom and ignorance.

vocabulary.definition: Diotima's step-by-step ascent from loving one beautiful body to loving all bodies, souls, laws, knowledge, and finally Beauty itself.
vocabulary.example: On the ladder of love, falling for one person's beauty is only the first rung.

vocabulary.definition: Originally (from Marsilio Ficino in the 1400s) love that rises through a person toward beauty and the divine; today usually means a non-sexual friendship.
vocabulary.example: For Plato, Platonic love was passionate and spiritual, not merely the absence of romance.

vocabulary.definition: The belief that the soul (the thinking, living self) survives the death of the body; defended by Socrates in the Phaedo.
vocabulary.example: Socrates' final argument for the immortality of the soul claims that the soul, which brings life, cannot admit death.

vocabulary.definition: The argument that learning is remembering knowledge of the Forms the soul had before birth, so the soul existed before the body.
vocabulary.example: Recognizing that two sticks are not perfectly equal is, for Plato, evidence for the argument from recollection.

vocabulary.definition: Hatred or distrust of reasoning and argument, which Socrates warns against in the Phaedo.
vocabulary.example: After several bad arguments, it is tempting to slide into misology, but Socrates says the fault lies in our skill, not in reason.

thinkingExercise.title: Your Own Ladder
thinkingExercise.prompt: Diotima claims that love, properly understood, draws us from particular beautiful things toward what is lasting and good. Test her idea against your own experience.
steps: Write about one person, place, work of art or activity you have loved deeply. What exactly drew you to it at first?

Did that love lead you anywhere beyond itself? For example, did loving one piece of music make you love music in general, or did loving someone make you care more about kindness or fairness? Map your own 'ladder', however short.
Now take Aristophanes' side. Is there something about the particular person or thing you loved that could not be replaced by anything 'higher'? Write down what would be lost.
Finally, consider the Phaedo: does the thought of death make the things you love more or less valuable to you? Write a short paragraph explaining why.

summary: The Symposium is a series of speeches praising Love at a drinking party in 416 BCE; the Phaedo recounts Socrates' last conversation and death in 399 BCE.
Aristophanes' myth says humans were split in half by Zeus, so love is the desire and pursuit of our lost wholeness.
Diotima teaches that Love is a needy daimon, that it desires to possess the good forever, and that it seeks immortality by giving birth in beauty, in body or soul.
The ladder of love rises from one beautiful body to all bodies, souls, laws, knowledge and finally Beauty itself, a Form; this is the original meaning of Platonic love.
In the Phaedo, philosophy is practice for dying, and Socrates gives the cyclical, recollection, affinity and final arguments for the soul's immortality.
Simmias' harmony objection and Cebes' weaver objection remain powerful, and most modern philosophers find none of the arguments decisive.

quiz.question: In Aristophanes' myth, why did Zeus cut the original humans in half?
options: To punish them for refusing to sacrifice to the gods
To create the first philosophers
To weaken them, because they were proud and attacked the gods
Because Apollo asked him to make humans more beautiful
quiz.explanation: The round humans were so strong that they tried to attack the gods, so Zeus weakened them by splitting them, leaving each half searching for the other.

quiz.question: Why does Socrates argue that Love cannot itself be beautiful?
options: Because Love desires beauty, and we only desire what we lack
Because the gods are never beautiful
Because Aristophanes proved that love is comic
Because beauty belongs only to the body, and Love is a soul
quiz.explanation: If Love is desire for beautiful things, it must lack them. This is why Diotima concludes Love is a needy go-between, not a perfect god.

quiz.question: Historians have confirmed that Diotima was a famous priestess whose life is well documented in many ancient sources.
quiz.explanation: Diotima appears nowhere outside Plato's Symposium, and many scholars think Plato invented her.

quiz.question: According to Diotima, why do mortals desire to 'give birth in beauty'?
options: Because the gods command humans to have children
Because creating children, poems or laws is a mortal's way of reaching for immortality
Because beautiful things are easier to sell
Because Love is the child of Aphrodite and must honor her
quiz.explanation: Love wants to possess the good forever. Since mortals die, they seek immortality by leaving offspring of body or soul behind them.

quiz.question: What is the highest step on the ladder of love?
options: Loving one beautiful body
Loving the beauty of laws and institutions
Loving all beautiful souls equally
Beholding Beauty itself, eternal and unchanging
quiz.explanation: The ascent ends with a vision of Beauty itself, which is a Form; laws, souls and bodies are lower rungs.

quiz.question: Which modern situation best illustrates Aristophanes' view of love rather than Diotima's?
options: A couple who say their relationship pushed them both to become kinder and braver
An artist whose love for one painting led her to study all of art history
A student who falls in love with mathematics and devotes her life to it
Someone who says they finally feel whole because they found 'the one' meant for them
quiz.explanation: Feeling completed by one's destined other half is Aristophanes' myth. The other options describe growth and ascent, which fits Diotima.

quiz.question: In the Phaedo, Socrates says that philosophy is a kind of practice for dying.
quiz.explanation: Since death separates soul from body, and philosophy tries to free the soul from bodily distractions, the philosopher's life is a rehearsal for death.

quiz.question: Simmias' objection compares the soul to:
options: A cloak that outlasts its weaver
Smoke that scatters in the wind
The attunement of a lyre, which is destroyed when the lyre is broken
A shadow on the wall of a cave
quiz.explanation: If the soul is like a harmony of the body's parts, it would perish with the body. The cloak image belongs to Cebes' objection.

quiz.question: Which argument for immortality relies on the claim that learning is really remembering?
options: The cyclical argument
The argument from recollection
The affinity argument
The final argument
quiz.explanation: The argument from recollection says we know Forms like Equality that we never encountered in this life, so the soul must have existed before birth.

quiz.question: The original meaning of 'Platonic love' was simply a friendship with no passion in it.
quiz.explanation: Ficino's phrase described a passionate love that rises through a person toward beauty and the divine. The modern meaning of non-sexual friendship is a later narrowing.

goDeeper.body:
One of the richest modern debates about the *Symposium* concerns whether the ladder of love is cold. Gregory Vlastos, in a famous essay, 'The Individual as an Object of Love in Plato', argued that Plato's lover loves people only insofar as they display beauty and goodness, so that the 'whole person', with their flaws and uniqueness, is never the true object of love. Martha Nussbaum, in *The Fragility of Goodness*, read Alcibiades' drunken speech as Plato's own acknowledgment of what the ascent costs: the passionate, risky, particular love that makes us vulnerable. Others defend Plato, arguing that the ladder does not discard earlier loves but transforms them, so that the lover still loves the beloved, only more wisely.

The *Phaedo* raises different questions. Its arguments rely heavily on the theory of Forms, and its 'final argument' is still debated: even if the soul cannot be dead while it exists, why can't it simply cease to exist? Socrates insists that what is deathless must also be indestructible, but many commentators find that step too quick. The harmony objection also had a long future. It anticipates the view, common in neuroscience and philosophy of mind today (Day 84), that the mind is something the brain does rather than a separate thing.

Finally, both dialogues raise the question of how much of the 'Socrates' we read is the historical man. The Phaedo's confident doctrine of Forms and immortality sits uneasily with the Apology's Socrates, who says he does not know whether death is dreamless sleep or a journey to another place (Day 10).

readings.title: Symposium
readings.author: Plato (trans. Alexander Nehamas and Paul Woodruff)
readings.note: Short and very readable. Aristophanes' speech is around 189c–193d, Diotima's teaching from about 201d to 212a, Alcibiades' entrance at 212d.

readings.title: Phaedo
readings.author: Plato (trans. G. M. A. Grube)
readings.note: Read the opening on philosophy as practice for death (to about 69e), the objections around 85e–88b, and the death scene from 115b to the end.

readings.title: The Fragility of Goodness
readings.author: Martha C. Nussbaum
readings.note: Chapter 6 offers a famous reading of Alcibiades' speech and what the ladder of love might leave behind.

readings.title: Plato's Symposium: The Ethics of Desire
readings.author: Frisbee C. C. Sheffield
readings.note: A clear scholarly study of Diotima's teaching, the idea of 'giving birth in beauty' and how the ladder of love works.

questions: Is it a flaw or a strength of Diotima's ladder that it moves the lover beyond any single beloved person?
Which of Socrates' arguments for immortality do you find most and least convincing, and why?
Does Simmias' harmony objection still work today, if we replace 'lyre' with 'brain'?
